questions.question: In the context of RL for LLMs, which statement best distinguishes online (on-policy) from offline (off-policy) data collection?
questions.choice_A: Online data is generated by the current policy during training, whereas offline data is collected from a different policy or a static dataset.
questions.choice_B: Online data is always higher quality than offline data because it comes from human annotators.
questions.choice_C: Offline data is generated by the current policy, while online data is gathered from historical logs.
questions.choice_D: Offline data can only be used for supervised learning, not RL.

questions.question: Which of the following is a primary risk when training a policy purely from offline data in LLM RL?
questions.choice_A: Excessive use of GPUs due to frequent sampling.
questions.choice_B: Distributional shift causing the learned policy to perform poorly when deployed on new prompts.
questions.choice_C: Inability to incorporate any human feedback.
questions.choice_D: Over-exploration due to high sampling temperature.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a replay buffer in iterative RL pipelines for LLMs?
questions.choice_A: To store model checkpoints for reproducibility across different runs.
questions.choice_B: To maintain a record of gradient updates for debugging numerical stability.
questions.choice_C: To retain past trajectories so that training can mix historical and fresh samples, stabilizing learning.
questions.choice_D: To compress token sequences to reduce memory footprint during inference.

questions.question: In iterative RL with reward model updates, what is a common stability issue when the reward model and policy are updated too aggressively in lockstep?
questions.choice_A: The policy becomes too deterministic and cannot be evaluated.
questions.choice_B: Gradient vanishing in the transformer’s attention blocks.
questions.choice_C: Underfitting to the pretraining distribution.
questions.choice_D: Feedback loops where the policy exploits transient reward model quirks, leading to oscillations or reward hacking.

questions.question: Which practice best mitigates overfitting the policy to a stale reward model during an iterative loop?
questions.choice_A: Periodically refreshing the reward model with newly labeled or preference data and revalidating on a held-out set.
questions.choice_B: Increasing the batch size indefinitely to average out gradients.
questions.choice_C: Turning off entropy regularization to encourage exploitation.
questions.choice_D: Using only offline data from pretraining corpora.

questions.question: When mixing historical and fresh data, which strategy helps control distributional shift during policy training?
questions.choice_A: Discarding all old data after each policy update.
questions.choice_B: Using a prioritized replay buffer that samples more from recent trajectories while still retaining some diverse historical data.
questions.choice_C: Training solely on synthetic self-play data to ensure consistency.
questions.choice_D: Freezing the tokenizer to prevent vocabulary drift.

questions.question: In on-policy RL for LLMs, how does exploration commonly manifest during sampling?
questions.choice_A: By increasing the embedding dimensionality to encourage novelty.
questions.choice_B: By lowering the learning rate to slow convergence.
questions.choice_C: By adjusting sampling parameters like temperature and top-$p$ to diversify generated trajectories.
questions.choice_D: By resetting positional encodings at each step.

questions.question: Which evaluation design best tracks true progress in an iterative RL loop where both the policy and reward model change over time?
questions.choice_A: Evaluating only with the latest reward model on the latest policy.
questions.choice_B: Evaluating only with human annotators on randomly chosen prompts.
questions.choice_C: Using a moving average of reward scores produced by the current reward model.
questions.choice_D: Interleaving evaluations against fixed, time-stamped benchmarks and human preference tests while also tracking reward under multiple frozen reward model snapshots.

questions.question: Why might an off-policy dataset collected from early-stage policies hinder learning when used without correction in later iterations?
questions.choice_A: It reduces the maximum sequence length available for training.
questions.choice_B: It introduces label leakage into the validation set.
questions.choice_C: Its action distribution may be far from the current policy’s, creating bias that leads the learner to suboptimal behaviors.
questions.choice_D: It prevents gradient clipping from working correctly.

questions.question: What is a practical benefit of checkpointing both the policy and reward model during iterative training?
questions.choice_A: It eliminates the need for any form of evaluation.
questions.choice_B: It enables rollback when a new update degrades performance, and supports consistent A/B comparisons across time.
questions.choice_C: It guarantees monotonic improvement of the policy.
questions.choice_D: It prevents catastrophic forgetting by itself.

questions.question: Which approach helps prevent reward hacking when the policy learns to exploit artifacts in the reward model?
questions.choice_A: Training with only a single, ever-changing reward model.
questions.choice_B: Removing KL penalties to allow unconstrained exploration.
questions.choice_C: Regularizing with KL divergence to a reference policy and periodically auditing with human preferences and adversarial test sets.
questions.choice_D: Shortening context length to limit exploitable patterns.

questions.question: During iterative RL, what is a key reason to maintain a fixed evaluation prompt set in addition to dynamic evaluation?
questions.choice_A: A fixed set guarantees generalization to unseen tasks.
questions.choice_B: Dynamic evaluation is always biased toward good results.
questions.choice_C: A fixed set provides a stable baseline for longitudinal comparisons, reducing confounds from changing data distributions.
questions.choice_D: It eliminates the need for reward modeling.

questions.question: How does mixing on-policy samples with curated offline data typically affect exploration and stability?
questions.choice_A: It decreases exploration while improving numerical stability of the optimizer.
questions.choice_B: It increases exploration while destabilizing the optimizer.
questions.choice_C: It balances exploration from fresh on-policy data with stability and coverage from diverse offline data.
questions.choice_D: It eliminates the need for any entropy regularization.

questions.question: Which engineering practice most directly improves throughput in an iterative RL pipeline for LLMs without changing learning dynamics?
questions.choice_A: Increasing the reward scale so gradients are larger.
questions.choice_B: Asynchronous batching of rollouts and scoring, with sharded sampling workers feeding a centralized learner.
questions.choice_C: Removing gradient clipping to avoid kernel overhead.
questions.choice_D: Using a larger context window than needed.

questions.question: What is a common pitfall when evaluating a policy solely with the same reward model used for training?
questions.choice_A: It always underestimates the true capabilities of the model.
questions.choice_B: It can mask regressions because the policy may overfit to that reward model’s biases.
questions.choice_C: It makes human evaluation redundant and unreliable.
questions.choice_D: It prevents logging of token-level probabilities.

questions.question: Which strategy helps manage instability when jointly updating a reward model and policy?
questions.choice_A: Updating both continuously with no separation of timescales.
questions.choice_B: Randomly reinitializing the reward model each epoch.
questions.choice_C: Using different timescales: update the policy more frequently and the reward model less frequently, validating each reward update before rollout expansion.
questions.choice_D: Disabling replay buffers to avoid stale data.

questions.question: In off-policy RL for LLMs, why might importance sampling or weighting be considered when using a replay buffer?
questions.choice_A: To reduce the number of parameters in the policy network.
questions.choice_B: To exactly match the tokenization scheme across datasets.
questions.choice_C: To correct for the mismatch between the behavior policy that generated data and the current policy, reducing bias in gradient estimates.
questions.choice_D: To force the model to ignore rare but valuable trajectories.

questions.question: What is a practical reason to version datasets, policies, and reward models in an iterative pipeline?
questions.choice_A: Versioning guarantees that evaluation will always improve.
questions.choice_B: It enables data lineage tracking, reproducibility of experiments, and precise attribution of regressions to specific changes.
questions.choice_C: It reduces GPU memory usage during backpropagation.
questions.choice_D: It makes human feedback unnecessary.

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates distributional shift in iterative RL for LLMs?
questions.choice_A: Training on multilingual data and evaluating on the same languages.
questions.choice_B: Using a fixed validation set from the training distribution.
questions.choice_C: Collecting online rollouts on new, harder prompts that differ from the offline training corpus, leading to unexpected failures.
questions.choice_D: Lowering the learning rate during fine-tuning.

questions.question: During iterative training, which safeguard helps ensure you can diagnose and recover from sudden drops in performance?
questions.choice_A: Only training with on-policy data to avoid stale samples.
questions.choice_B: Frequent checkpointing with metadata (config, seed, data hashes), plus automated canary evaluations and alerting on key metrics.
questions.choice_C: Disabling logging to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
questions.choice_D: Always accepting the latest model if its training reward increased.
